8.25

F. Review: Present tense

While you most likely feel comfortable using the present tense by now, it's important to keep in mind the ways in which English and German differ in how they use it.

To illustrate this we’ll use two familiar verbs:

arbeiten to work
schreiben to write

F.1

Ask yourself how the specific forms used in the following sentences (e.g. work / works / working) affect the meanings of the verbs in context:

She usually works in Firestone or in her room.

She’s working on her thesis. She's writing it right now, in fact.

Does she work alone or with friends? Does she always write multiple drafts?

Is she writing it at the moment?

She’ll work more on it later. She’ll write it over the weekend.

She’s been working on it since Monday. She’s been writing for days.

In each of these sentences, work and write combine with various auxiliaries and suffixes to express different nuances of meaning:

  • Statements:

    general: She works …

    process: She is working … (emphasis: right now / in process)

  • Questions:

    general: Does she always write …?

    process: Is she working …?

  • Future tense: She’ll write …

  • Present perfect: She’s been working …

Notice that the only context in which you find an English present-tense verb stripped of all auxiliaries involves statements expressing general validity:

She works on her thesis at night.

She usually writes from 11pm to 2am.

English modal verbs are an exception to this last rule, in that they routinely appear without auxiliaries: She can work on it tonight. May I ask you a question? Must the paper be handed in tomorrow? But not always: Does the paper have to be handed in tomorrow?

(Good luck trying to explain this to a non-native speaker.)

F.1
label: F.1

content:
F.2

By contrast, German simply uses the present-tense form of the verb in all of these contexts:

  • Statements expressing both general validity and process:

    Sie arbeitet…

    Sie schreibt…

    She is working … / She works …

    She is writing … / She writes …

  • Questions expressing both general validity and process:

    Arbeitet sie…?

    Schreibt sie…?

    Does she work …? / Is she working …?

    Does she write …? / Is she writing …?

  • Statements and questions referring to the future (as long as future time is implied by the context):

    Sie arbeitet später daran.

    Sie schreibt es am Wochenende.

    She’ll work on it later.

    She’ll write it over the weekend.

    (German does, in fact, have a future tense form, which will be introduced in a later chapter; but whenever the context clearly points to future time, German speakers prefer to use the present tense.)

  • Present perfect tense (i.e., referring to something that began in the past but is ongoing in the present):

    Sie arbeitet seit Montag.

    Sie schreibt seit Tagen.

    She’s been working since Monday.

    She’s been writing for days.

    Notice that the action's starting point (since Monday) as well as its duration (for days), is expressed with seit, followed by the dative case.

G.1

plural

Remember:

  • If the verb stem ends in -d or -t, an -e- must be inserted before the endings -t and -st (e.g., arbeitet / arbeitest).

  • If the stem ends with -s, -z, or -ß, the du ending (-st) is reduced to -t (e.g., du heißt).

H. Review: Modal verbs


H.1

Modal verbs convey a “mode” (an attitude or posture) regarding the main verb in the clause, allowing you to communicate not merely that someone is doing something, but that the person must do it, or wants to do it, or can do it.

There are six modal verbs in German, one of which frequently appears in its subjunctive form, which is shown here in brackets:

dürfen to be allowed to; may (permission)
können to be able to; can
mögen to like [möchten would like to]
müssen to have to; must
sollen to be supposed to; should
wollen to want to

Points to keep in mind when using modal verbs:

  • Word order: Modal verbs function as V1 in the “sentence bracket,” meaning that they appear immediately after the first element of an independent clause. The infinitive linked to the modal verb functions as V2, appearing at the end of the clause:

    Heute Abend können wir vielleicht zusammen essen.

  • Conjugation: Modal verbs have irregular conjugations. All but one (sollen) undergo a change in the stem vowel in the forms for ich/du/er/sie/es; and the forms for ich as well as er/sie/es are identical — just the stem, with no ending.

  • Meaning: können/müssen/wollen correspond closely with their English equivalents can/must/want; but dürfen, sollen and mögen don’t map as easily onto English meanings, and you should review the explanations and examples in Chapter 6 to be sure you know how to use them.

  • Negation: Most modal verbs are negated simply by adding nicht, so that können + nicht means cannot, wollen + nicht means doesn’t want to, and so on. But müssen is a special case: Wir müssen nicht means We don't have to (i.e., not required); the stronger meaning must not (i.e., not permissible) is expressed by dürfen + nicht.

content:
H.3

The past tense of modal verbs is formed by adding endings to a past-tense modal stem (a stem ending with -t), which remains unchanged across all singular and plural forms:

durft-

was allowed to

konnt-

was able to; could

mocht-

liked to

musst-

had to

sollt-

was supposed to

wollt-

wanted to

The endings are applied to these stems (using können as an example) as follows:


können → konnt- was able to

singular

plural

first-person

ich konnte … I was able to

wir konnten … we were able to

second-person

du konntest … you were able to

ihr konntet … you (all) were able to

Sie konnten … you were able to

Sie konnten … you were able to

third-person

er / sie / es konnte …

he / she / it was able to

sie konnten … they were able to

Some examples with the other modal verbs:

Wir wollten mit dir gehen.

We wanted to go with you.

Er sollte zum Fußball-Training gehen, aber er konnte nicht.

He was supposed to go to soccer practice, but he couldn’t/wasn't able to.

Warum durftest du nicht spielen?

Why weren’t you allowed to play?

Ich musste heute nicht so früh aufstehen.

I didn’t have to get up so early today.

As the examples illustrate, modal verbs in the past tense function just like modal verbs in the present tense:

  • Word order: the same for both tenses: ___[V1] _____[V2]

  • Meaning: As in the present tense, sollten and durften require special attention (see Chapter 6); there is no past tense form for möchten.

  • Negation: past-tense modal verbs are also negated with nicht. They take the meanings you’d expect — except for mussten + nicht, which means didn’t have to.

H.4

Wissen isn’t a modal verb, but it conjugates like one. The stem undergoes a vowel shift (i → ei) in the forms for ich/du/er/sie/es. And like modal verbs, the forms for first-person (ich) and third-person (er/sie/es) are identical — just the stem, with no endings.


wissen to know (information)

singular

plural

first-person

ich weiß

wir wissen

second-person

du weißt [familiar]

Sie wissen [formal]

ihr wisst [familiar]

Sie wissen [formal]

third-person

er/sie/es weiß

sie/die Kinder wissen

Present perfect: hat … gewusst


Keep in mind:

  • Wissen means to know in the sense of knowing information — which includes short bits of information (telephone numbers, addresses, names) expressed as a direct object, as well as clauses such as Ich weiß, was du denkst. (You’ll learn how to form clauses like this in Chapter 9.)

  • It does not mean to know in the sense of being acquainted with someone. To express this, German uses kennen, which conjugates regularly: Ich kenne, du kennst, er/sie/es kennt, … — and the Perfect tense is hat … gekannt.
